notes.h: Reasons poverty continues in modern western society
notes.b: Poverty persists where income from work is low or missing and where the costs of living absorb whatever income there is.
points: Unemployment: a household with no earned income depends on State payments, which are normally lower than wages.
Long-term unemployment erodes skills, work habits and confidence, making re-entry to the labour market harder.
Low pay: unskilled and minimum-wage work often leaves full-time workers unable to afford an acceptable standard of living.
Limited education: early school leavers and people with few qualifications are concentrated in low-paid and insecure work.
Lone parenthood and large families: one income must cover food, housing and childcare for several people.
High housing and living costs: rent, mortgage repayments, energy and transport take a large share of low incomes.
Addiction and gambling: spending on alcohol, drugs or gambling diverts money from essentials and leads to debt.
Recession and industrial decline: the closure of a major employer removes jobs and the local businesses that depended on its workers' spending.
Globalisation and automation: production moved abroad or mechanised reduces demand for unskilled labour, mainly in manufacturing.

notes.h: The cycle of poverty (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Disadvantage is passed from one generation to the next, so poverty repeats itself unless something interrupts the pattern.
points: Children raised in low-income households often have less access to good education, health care and social networks than children from better-off families.
Some children from poorer families place less value on education, leave school early and move into unemployment or low-paid work.
Their own children are then born into the same financial conditions, so the pattern repeats across generations.
Each stage reinforces the next: low income means poorer housing and diet, which affect health and school attendance, which in turn limit later earnings.
Breaking the cycle requires intervention at the point where it repeats, for example early-years education, family support and access to training.

notes.h: Influence of social policy on poverty (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Social policy is the set of State decisions on welfare, housing, minimum pay, education and employment supports.
points: These decisions determine who is poor and for how long, because they set the income, housing and training available to each household.
Critics argue that welfare payments set below the cost of basic needs keep recipients in poverty.
Other critics argue that generous payments reduce the incentive to seek work and so sustain dependence on the State.
A minimum wage sets a legal floor for pay, so it directly determines what a full-time low-paid worker earns.
Housing policy affects poverty directly: the supply and cost of social and private rented housing decide how much of a low income is left after rent.
Support that is poorly targeted or changes often leaves gaps, so families move in and out of poverty rather than escaping it.

notes.h: Cycle of deprivation in families and geographical areas (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Deprivation is the lack of resources, services and opportunities that are normal in society, and it builds up over time.
points: In families, low income, low education and ill health limit the support parents can give children for learning, and children inherit the same limits.
Children in such families often have little contact with people in employment, so they grow up with few working role models.
In geographical areas, concentrated unemployment and dependence on welfare create employment blackspots, often after a major industry closes.
Services in those areas, such as shops, buses, schools and health centres, close as spending falls, making the area less attractive to employers and families.
Deprivation reinforces itself: an area losing population and skilled workers loses the tax base and demand that could sustain new employment.
Responses target the locality as well as the household: community education, transport, job creation and local services.

notes.b: The poverty trap is a situation in which taking up work brings little or no gain in net income.
points: A household moving from welfare into low-paid work loses payments and supports as earnings rise, so its net income increases very little.
Supports often withdrawn as earnings rise include housing assistance, medical card eligibility and, in some cases, child-related payments.
The costs of working, such as transport, childcare and work clothing, reduce the gain further.
When welfare is financially more rewarding than low-paid work, people have little incentive to take employment, which keeps them dependent.
Payments reduced gradually as earnings rise, rather than withdrawn all at once, lessen the trap; in-work payments such as the Working Family Payment are designed for low-paid working families.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on the individual
points: Stress, worry and fear about money, which can lead to depression and poor mental health.
Loss of status and self-esteem, and a feeling of worthlessness, which can reduce confidence to seek work or training.
Social isolation, because the cost of leisure, travel and social activities is beyond reach.
Poor diet, and poorly heated or damp housing, increase the risk of illness, and ill health can prevent people from working.
Dependence on alcohol, drugs or gambling as a means of escape, which adds to debt and poverty.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on families and children
points: Families may be unable to afford adequate food, clothing, heating and housing, and fall into rent, mortgage or utility arrears.
Financial pressure increases conflict and relationship strain, and can contribute to family breakdown.
Children may be unable to take part in school trips, sport or activities their peers attend, which affects belonging and self-esteem.
Children without a quiet place to study, books or internet access may fall behind in school.
Children growing up in poverty are more likely to leave school early with few qualifications, which limits their later earnings.
Poorer diet and access to health care can affect children's physical health and development.
Loss of a home forces children to move school and loses the stability that supports their learning.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on the community and the State
points: Higher demand for welfare, health and housing services increases the cost to the State.
Concentrated poverty can contribute to crime, anti-social behaviour and vandalism in an area.
Falling spending in poorer areas leads to shop closures and fewer local services, which reduces jobs further.
Poverty reduces the skills and productive capacity available to the economy.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which disadvantage, such as low education and income, is passed from one generation to the next and repeats.
The reinforcing process in which a lack of resources, services and opportunities in families or areas causes further disadvantage.
A situation in which moving from welfare into low-paid work brings little or no gain in net income because supports are withdrawn.
The State's decisions on welfare, housing, pay, education and employment, which shape who is poor and for how long.
The lack of resources, services and opportunities that are normal in society, and the exclusion that results.
An area with persistently high unemployment, often where a major industry has closed.
Being unable to take part in activities considered normal in society because of low income and limited resources.

factCards.term: Four reasons poverty continues in modern western society
factCards.definition: Unemployment and low pay; limited education and qualifications; high housing and living costs; lone parenthood and large families relying on one income.

factCards.term: Three effects of poverty on children
factCards.definition: Early school leaving with few qualifications; poorer health and development; low self-esteem and reduced participation in school life.

factCards.term: Costs that can cancel out the gain from low-paid work
factCards.definition: Transport, childcare and work clothing, plus the loss of supports such as housing assistance or a medical card.

factCards.term: Two ways disadvantage reinforces itself within families and areas
factCards.definition: Within families, disadvantage passes from parents to children through limited support for learning and work; within areas, concentrated unemployment and closing services reinforce each other.

factCards.term: Effect of poverty on family finances
factCards.definition: Rent, mortgage, utility and credit arrears build up when income cannot cover essential bills.

factCards.term: Signs that an area has concentrated joblessness and decline
factCards.definition: Persistently high unemployment, long-term welfare dependence and the closure of a major local employer or industry.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the poverty trap and describe one way it discourages people from taking up work.
questions.model: The poverty trap is a situation in which moving from welfare into work brings little or no gain in net income. Earnings from low-paid work cause payments or supports to be withdrawn. Supports that may be lost include housing assistance and medical card eligibility. The extra costs of working, such as childcare and travel, reduce the gain further. Because welfare can be financially more rewarding than low-paid work, people have little incentive to take up employment and remain dependent on the State.

questions.prompt: Examine why poverty persists in modern western societies, and assess how the cycle of deprivation and social policy contribute to it.
questions.model: Reasons for persistence: unemployment and low pay leave households without adequate income; limited education and qualifications restrict people to insecure work; high housing and living costs absorb low incomes; lone parenthood and large families depend on one income; addiction and debt drain resources; recession and industrial decline remove jobs; globalisation and automation reduce demand for unskilled labour. Cycle of deprivation: in families, low income and low education limit the support parents give children, who inherit the same disadvantage; in geographical areas, concentrated unemployment and dependence on welfare create employment blackspots, and closing services reduce the area's attractiveness, which deepens decline. Social policy: welfare payments set below the cost of basic needs can keep recipients in poverty, while generous payments are criticised for reducing the incentive to work; the minimum wage sets the floor for low pay; housing policy determines the rent burden; the poverty trap arises when withdrawal of supports offsets earnings; policy that is poorly targeted or changes often leaves families moving in and out of poverty. Assessment: the cycle of deprivation and social policy interact, since policy can either break or reinforce the cycle through education, housing and employment supports.
